items.title: Russia’s Kerch Bridge Road Vehicle Span Has Been Destroyed By Ukraine
items.summary:
UPDATE: 12:40 AM EST— 

The road vehicle span of the Kerch Strait Bridge has been destroyed by Ukraine. Imagery now circulating after the sun came up shows the bridge section that was struck yesterday has now been totally dropped in an overnight attack. Ukraine has been trying to accomplish this for years and has finally succeeded. It is not clear what level of damage was done to the rail span that sits next to it. It’s quite possible, if not probable, that this section will be attacked in the coming hours. 

Images show that the main span and arch of the Kerch Bridge were destroyed in overnight strikes. https://t.co/Jr661DN6Tu pic.twitter.com/YbrZcZAsCt 

— Liveuamap (@Liveuamap) November 17, 2026 

Fuck yeah!!!! pic.twitter.com/IjK7DbX5ap 

— capt. Wild Bill Kelso (@_wild_billkelso) November 17, 2026 

The wreckage from the destroyed span is also blocking access for large vessels to the Sea of Azov, which will also strangle Russian logistics.

We also are seeing a video of an FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile with what appears to be man-in-the-loop control making its attack run on this part of the bridge. We cannot confirm the authenticity of the video at this time, but the FP-5 carries a massive 2,500lb warhead that would be capable of this kind of damage if it hits at the right spot. 

Video footage published by the Armed Forces of Ukraine shows the moment right before a Ukrainian-produced FP-5 “Flamingo” ground-launched cruise missile struck the Kerch Strait Bridge. pic.twitter.com/fxOOIWIQkU 

— OSINTdefender (@sentdefender) November 17, 2026

items.t: Kerch Bridge Struck For The Second Time In Less Than 24 Hours: Russia

items.title: Russia’s Prized Kerch Bridge Struck In Ukrainian Drone Onslaught (Updated)
items.summary:
The Kerch Bridge, one of Russia’s most strategically important and heavily defended pieces of infrastructure, spanning the Kerch Strait between Krasnodar Krai in Russia and the Kerch Peninsula of Crimea, has been struck again. The latest attacks came amid a massive Ukrainian overnight offensive that Moscow says involved 1,336 long-range drones.

Update: The Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov reported a second attack on the bridge in less than 24 hours. 

The Russian-installed head of occupied Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the crossing, which includes both automotive and rail lanes, had been targeted earlier today, announcing temporary traffic restrictions while authorities assessed the situation. 

A satellite image provided to TWZ by Vantor and also used at the top of this story showing the Kerch Bridge after the latest attack. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor Satellite image ©2026 Vantor

The attack reportedly occurred at approximately 5:38 a.m. local time, with a Ukrainian one-way attack drone striking one of the bridge’s arches. Russian air defenses were reportedly engaging incoming drones around the structure.

Video purportedly showing the moment of the attack includes the appearance of a straight-winged, propeller-driven drone with the twin booms and inverted-V tail that is a feature of several different Ukrainian strike drones.

items.title: First F-15EXs Arrive At Kadena Air Base In Japan, 25 Now Delivered To The USAF
items.summary:
The U.S. Air Force now has two F-15EX Eagle II fighters permanently forward-deployed at Kadena Air Base on the Japanese island of Okinawa. The 18th Wing has been awaiting the arrival of F-15EXs as replacements for its retired F-15C/D Eagles for years now. This milestone also highlights the continued expansion of the overall Air Force Eagle II fleet , which has now grown to 25 jets.

The 18th Wing announced that its first F-15EXs had touched down at Kadena yesterday. Prime contractor Boeing confirmed today that those jets were the 22nd and 23rd Eagle IIs produced (EX22 and EX23) in posts across its social media accounts. The expectation is that 36 F-15EXs will eventually be based in Japan, with 18 each assigned to the 44th and 67th Fighter Squadrons. 

An F-15EX Eagle II seen about to land at Kadena Air Base on November 15, 2026. USAF 

Boeing also confirmed to TWZ directly today that 25 F-15EXs have been delivered to the Air Force. This includes all of the jets in the first and second production lots. Lot 3 deliveries are now underway. The total Air Force Eagle IIs fleet is now set to reach 267 airframes, roughly double what the program of record was in 2025. 

EX22, the first Japan-bound Eagle II, had left Boeing’s plant in St. Louis in September and traveled first to Portland Air National Guard Base in Oregon. The base is collocated with Portland International Airport and is home to the Oregon Air National Guard’s 142nd Wing, the first unit to fly combat-coded F-15EXs. The 142nd has been central to coordinating and preparing the way for the deployment of Eagle IIs to…
items.t: First F-15EXs Arrive At Kadena Air Base In Japan, 25 Now Delivered To The USAF

items.title: Air Force bets on hybrid-electric aircraft for transport
items.summary:
The Air Force is pitching in nearly $5 million to help a Virginia-based aerospace company bring a 9-seat hybrid-electric airplane to flight—and to evaluate its potential use in combat.

A $4.7 million other transaction agreement contract from AFWERX will help Electra develop its EL9 prototype aircraft, building on the company’s existing EL2 two-seat prototype.

The EL9 is a small aircraft, comparable to a Cessna Caravan or Pilatus PC-12. Its size, combined with the ability to take off and land in just 150 feet, could make it good to use for special operations. 

“The USAF has always been interested in what new technology can bring to the battlefield, and the new contract will let it test what an ultra-[short take off and landing] aircraft can do in service,” said Douglas Royce, senior aerospace and power systems analyst for Forecast International. “The contract isn’t a signal that the USAF is ready to acquire this type of aircraft, but the vulnerability of traditional air bases to missile attack may encourage the use of distributed operations in combat zones. Operating an ultra-STOL platform from short or improvised runways may be a part of that concept.”

“The special forces use would make sense because having a…
items.t: Air Force bets on hybrid-electric aircraft for transport

items.title: First permanently assigned F-15EXs touch down at Kadena Air Base
items.summary:
A Japan air base became the first American installation abroad to receive two permanently assigned F-15EX Eagle IIs and the second-ever Air Force location to field the fighter jet . 

Kadena Air Base , located in Okinawa, Japan, received two of the fighter aircraft Sunday as the Air Force strives to increase U.S. airpower in the Pacific, according to a recent service release , especially as the base continues to replace its F-15C/D fleet.

“[F-15EXs] strengthen our ability to deter aggression, respond to emerging threats and defend Japan alongside our allies and partners,” 18th Wing Commander Brig. Gen. John Gallemore said in the release.

“Their permanent presence at Kadena reinforces our commitment to the U.S.-Japan alliance and ensures we continue to bring advanced combat capabilities to one of the most strategically important regions in the world,” he continued.

In November 2022, the base first began withdrawing its legacy F-15C/D aircraft after four decades of service. The transition included rotational deployments of fourth- and fifth-generation fighters to maintain a fighter presence while maintainers, operators and mission support airmen sought the expertise needed to utilize a new platform as soon as it reaches operational capability, the release says.

Two years after the Oregon Air National Guard received theirs, the F-15EXs at Kadena are expected to increase the base’s ability to conduct counterair operations and boost the service’s forward-deployed capabilities.

With advanced avionics, modernized electronic warfare systems and heightened weapons-carrying…
items.t: First permanently assigned F-15EXs touch down at Kadena Air Base

items.title: DoD restores parental access to teens’ medical records
items.summary:
Military parents will be able to view their teenagers’ Defense Department electronic health records more easily starting Wednesday — a change parents have said is necessary to guide health decisions for their children. 

Beginning Nov. 18, dependent children ages 13-18 will be able to go into the MHS Genesis portal and grant permission for their parents to view their medical records. Previously, parents had to go into patient administration offices at their military hospital or clinic and have their teenage children sign a consent form for parents to have access. 

The cumbersome process and restrictions, which went into effect in 2023 , have vexed military parents, according to Army Surgeon General Lt. Gen. Mary Izaguirre. 

“The parents don’t have access to [records] based on the current departmental policy, and then the children don’t have ID cards to sign in to get into [the Defense Enrollment and Eligibility Records System] … so there’s this space,” Izaguirre said Oct. 13 during a forum for families at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting. 

Parental access to minor medical records largely depends on state and federal regulations. An update in 2023 to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act’s (HIPAA) privacy rules modified the circumstances under which a person’s health information can be disclosed under federal law. 

The change, which followed the Supreme Court’s decision in 2022 to overturn Roe v. Wade, prohibited doctors, insurance companies and other health organizations from disclosing patient information to state officials for…
items.t: DoD restores parental access to teens’ medical records

items.title: U.S. Army Now Wants Concrete Bunkers For Troops In Israel, Saudi Arabia And Lebanon
items.summary:
In order to better protect personnel, U.S. Army Central (ARCENT) is looking to replace converted shipping containers with concrete bunkers as shelters at several locations in Israel, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia. The effort underscores questions about why more investments in physical hardening were not made in the region well before the current conflict. 

The Army’s search for companies that can build the new bunkers also came just days before 60 Minutes had interviews with family members of troops killed in Kuwait and a soldier who was there raising concerns about why more was not done to provide even basic hardening at a base where six soldiers died in an Iranian drone attack. Iranian attacks across the region also destroyed and damaged aircraft , radars and other equipment, and did billions in damage to infrastructure used by the U.S. military.

For years now , TWZ has been highlighting how the lack of hardened infrastructure at American military facilities abroad and at home creates worrisome vulnerabilities .

“Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace non-standard personnel protection shelters (e.g., converted shipping containers) and provide standardized precast reinforced concrete Indirect Fire (IDF) bunkers,” according to a sources sought synopsis posted Nov. 13 on the U.S. government’s main online contracting portal. “The objective is to safeguard U.S. and Coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in the USCENTCOM [U.S. Central Command] Area…
items.t: U.S. Army Now Wants Concrete Bunkers For Troops In Israel, Saudi Arabia And Lebanon

items.title: Air Force training chief’s No. 1 priority: Be more like the Marines
items.summary:
The three-star general overseeing training for the Air Force and Space Force said Monday that he’s serious about getting newly trained airmen to emulate the culture of another service: the Marine Corps.

In a wide-ranging discussion hosted by The Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, Lt. Gen. Clark Quinn called an identity shift his top command priority.

“If you find a Marine, where they’re active-duty, retired, doesn’t matter, and you ask them, ‘Hey, what do you do?’ Their answer is, ‘I’m a Marine,'” Quinn said. If you ask the same of an airman, he added, you’re more likely to hear him or her identify by their specific career field. 

“Part of what we are trying to do in forging airmen is to get that fundamental underpinning that is, what does it mean to be an airman,” he said. “I don’t know that by the end of my time here, an airman is going to go, ‘I’m an airman,’ but that’s the mentality that we’re trying to drive into it.”

The Air Force has been emphasizing its cultural identity – what service members sometimes call “airmindedness” – in other ways. A Basic Military Training overhaul currently underway gives the most junior trainees the opportunity, for example, to load and rearm an F-16 Fighting Falcon, emphasizing every airman’s role in providing airpower to the joint force.

In a September interview, officers leading that effort told Military Times that the added intensity and hands-on learning was making trainees more curious about combat scenarios and prompting them to think critically and independently about their training.

While it’s not a further effort…
items.t: Air Force training chief’s No. 1 priority: be more like the Marines

items.title: US Army takes ‘urgent’ action to build concrete bunkers across the Middle East
items.summary:
Fearing for the safety of American troops, the U.S. Army will build concrete bunkers across the Middle East.

The Army wants 17 bunkers capable of remaining intact through indirect fire attacks, such as from missiles and drones. Ten bunkers are planned for Israel, five in Saudi Arabia and two in Lebanon, according to an Army notice posted Friday.

The bunkers are meant to replace current personnel shelters made of converted shipping containers, the notice says.

“Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace nonstandard personnel protection shelters (e.g., converted shipping containers) and provide standardized, precast, reinforced concrete Indirect Fire bunkers,” states the Army’s Sources Sought notice . The deadline for companies to respond to the notice is Nov. 25.

“The objective is to safeguard U.S. and coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in [U.S. Central Command] Area of Responsibility,” the notice continues.

The project comes after Iranian missiles and drones devastated multiple American bases in the Persian Gulf and killed at least 23 personnel . This includes a March 2026 strike on an Army command post in Kuwait that killed six service members. Subsequent reports allege that the site was poorly protected against aerial bombardment.

The Army did not specify the exact locations of the new bunkers.

“Specific base installation names and coordinates” will be released only to eligible contractors once the actual solicitation is released,” the…
items.t: US Army takes ‘urgent’ action to build concrete bunkers across the Middle East

items.title: Services to report number of troops affected by ‘emergency’ living conditions
items.summary:
Within five days of a new Pentagon directive, all military services must confirm their compliance by attempting to resolve emergent living conditions within 24 hours or relocate the affected service member.

Departments are required to inspect all service members’ rooms and report to the Barracks Task Force the number of service members currently affected by “emergency” conditions, relocations completed and rooms vacated, according to a Nov. 10 memo signed by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

By Friday, all services are also required to report to the task force any actions taken to fix the conditions, along with projected timelines for restoring the rooms to “habitable occupancy,” and any policy or resource barriers that need Pentagon resolution.

“Unit integrity, room availability, manpower shortages, maintenance delays, lack of funding or conflicting Military Department policies do not justify continued occupancy of unacceptable housing,” the memo reads.

Barracks Task Force Senior Advisor Dakota Meyer says military leaders have less than a week to move any service member living in emergency conditions in unaccompanied housing. 

The Barracks Task Force, led by Medal of Honor recipient and Marine Corps reservist Dakota Meyer, stood up last year in an effort to address the military’s subpar living conditions. As Hegseth’s senior advisor, Meyer is traveling to installations across the country, looking at their barracks, meeting with service members and identifying how to curtail any issues blocking the resolutions. 

So far, Meyer has been to seven installations and is…
items.t: Services to report number of troops affected by ‘emergency’ living conditions

items.title: New Bow Sonar Dome For Heavily Damaged Submarine USS Connecticut Seen For The First Time (Updated)
items.summary:
TWZ has obtained new details about the ongoing repairs to the Seawolf class submarine USS Connecticut following collision with an underwater seamount in the South China Sea in 2021. The Navy had been looking at a roughly three-year timeline for the construction of a replacement bow sonar dome. In the end, it took just under a year for it to be built. The overall schedule for repairs to Connecticut has suffered delays, and we were the first to report that the boat is now not expected to return to service until next summer.

Editor’s note: After this story was published, Janicki Industries reached out to us to ask that the image of the dome be taken down while an additional review is conducted. Out of courtesy, we agreed, and we will repost it if and when it is fully approved. 

Janicki Industries produced the new bow sonar dome in approximately 10 months and delivered it to the Navy in 2024, the company told us today. Janicki has a history of producing “sonar domes and precision machined hardware” for U.S. nuclear submarine programs, according to its website . It has also supported various high-profile aerospace programs, including the B-21 Raider bomber and F-35 Joint Strike Fighter . 

Connecticut ’s bow had initially remained attached, at least to some degree, following the collision five years ago, according to a heavily redacted Navy report on the accident . However, the entire bow structure subsequently broke away as the submarine limped to Guam . The boat then sailed to San Diego, California , and then to the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance…
items.t: New Bow Sonar Dome For Heavily Damaged Submarine USS Connecticut Seen For The First Time

The soldier was originally arrested in the United Kingdom, where it was expected he would face an indictment over the alleged national security breach, but now he may face espionage charges in the United States, an Army official said.

Brandon Tyner, 41, who was assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters. The headquarters is a British-led unit with 20 countries assigned to it.

Army officials said Tyner was arrested on suspicion of violating sections of the U.K.’s National Security Act of 2023 for obtaining, copying, recording or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

items.title: Europe hunts for Palantir alternatives as militaries seek to limit US dependence
items.summary:
As Europe’s defense ministries look to limit dependency on American technology and major software company Palantir Technologies for critical military functions, a growing number of firms within the region are competing for their business. 

Last week, Germany’s Helsing unveiled military intelligence software called Clarity. It is part of a broader market for AI-powered systems designed to accelerate military decision-making by helping sift through vast quantities of data to identify threats and recommend action, including targeting and attacks.

But Europe currently lacks an exact equivalent that matches Palantir’s scale, deployment footprint and operational experience, some government and military officials say. 

That gives European militaries a dilemma: pursue homegrown systems that promise greater autonomy but may be less mature, or rely on a proven platform despite concerns about long-term strategic dependence.

The Trump administration has pushed Europe to take on much greater responsibility for its own security as Washington scales back its military presence in the region, and has placed pressure on the transatlantic NATO alliance. 

European officials face similar trade-offs between autonomy and capability across a range of military capabilities, including in the area of satellite communications, which is dominated by Elon Musk’s US company SpaceX. 

Ukraine last week reported further significant disruptions of its access to SpaceX, affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

France, a vocal advocate for European autonomy, is developing…
items.t: Europe hunts for Palantir alternatives as militaries seek to limit US dependence

items.title: Destroyers USS Spruance, USS Michael Murphy return from extended combat deployments
items.summary:
Two Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyers that played an integral role Middle East military operations during the Iran war returned to their homeports on Friday.

The USS Michael Murphy and USS Spruance docked at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii, and Naval Base San Diego, California, respectively. The Murphy deployed for 11 months while the Spruance deployed for 12.

“Leading the ship and crew has been the honor of a lifetime,” said Cmdr. Leigh R. Tate, commanding officer of Spruance. “Spruance sailors made a difference.”

Cmdr. David Nicolas, commanding officer of Michael Murphy, praised his crew for “defeating incoming air and surface threats” and “leading operations through contested choke points.”

The Spruance was deployed as part of the USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group, while the Murphy operated as part of Carrier Strike Group 3 under Destroyer Squadron 21, sailing alongside the Spruance and Lincoln.

Both ships assisted with combat military operations during Operation Epic Fury and the Iran war, and helped enforce the maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Spruance eliminated 12 unmanned aerial vehicles, four anti-ship cruise missiles and launched Tomahawk Land-Attack Cruise Missiles at Iranian targets. 

In total, the destroyer logged 43 underway replenishments that successfully provided 8.6 million gallons of fuel.

It also helped facilitate 190 sorties and 1,150 flight hours for its embarked Helicopter Maritime Strike Squadron Seven One.

Iranian government officials have claimed that munitions launched from the USS Spruance on Feb.…
items.t: Destroyers USS Spruance, USS Michael Murphy return from extended combat deployments

items.summary:
The director of the Marine Corps’ Tactical Training Exercise Control Group at Marine Air-Ground Task Force Training Command, Twentynine Palms, California, was relieved from his post this month without explanation, Task & Purpose confirmed.

Col. Eric Meador was removed from command of Tactical Training Exercise Control Group, a major training group that stages combined arms drills for Marines in Marine Air-Ground Task Forces, on Nov. 9. A Marine Corps spokesperson confirmed on Sunday that Meador had been relieved. No reason was given for his removal, with the Marine Corps citing the “administrative nature of this action” as the reason for the lack of additional information. His biography was scrubbed from the group’s website.

items.title: US and Russia to oppose talks on limiting autonomous weapons
items.summary:
Major arms producers the United States and Russia look set to oppose a push at a global meeting in Geneva this week to launch negotiations on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, diplomats and rights groups said.

The rise of artificial intelligence has boosted development of drones, robots, tanks, submarines and other military hardware capable of killing without human involvement. Semi-autonomous, AI-assisted weapons have already been used in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East, despite ethical concerns.

The UN-hosted meeting from Monday is due to decide whether to start talks for a legally binding pact on prohibitions and regulations for Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS). 

But while most of the 128 states party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons support that, major military nations including the U.S., Russia and Israel oppose it, arguing that existing humanitarian law is sufficient.

In a video message, the UN secretary-general urged states to agree to move towards negotiating a legally binding instrument including clear prohibitions and restrictions. 

“The nature of warfare is changing. New technologies — including autonomous weapon systems — present new humanitarian, legal, ethical and security challenges,” Antonio Guterres said. 

But Russia stymied the start of talks on Monday with its objection to a procedural rule allowing observers, including the EU and non-governmental organisations, to take the floor. Delegates including Ireland and Canada opposed that.

The International Committee of the Red Cross, along with the pope, has also…
items.t: US and Russia to oppose talks on limiting autonomous weapons

items.title: The secret terms of Trump’s Venezuelan oil deal
items.summary:
This story was originally published by ProPublica.

In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C. 

ProPublica has reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The document reveals carefully constructed terms that favor U.S. interests at every turn and cements the power of a small group of people handpicked by the Trump administration to govern and profit from the deal. The role of the Venezuelan government and the potential benefits to its people are largely absent from the text.

One of the most criticized aspects of Trump’s announcement has been his choice of a partner: Alejandro Betancourt, a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries. 

The Trump administration is taking a 35% stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners, by acquiring shares in a Barbados-registered parent company. The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement. 

The agreement…
items.t: The secret terms of Trump’s Venezuelan oil deal

items.title: Troops in unsafe barracks can get temporary housing on or off base, Pentagon says
items.summary:
Troops living in barracks with “emergency conditions” that pose health or safety risks can get temporary lodging on or off base, according to new rules set by the Pentagon. 

In a Nov. 10 memo, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth directed the services to follow barracks standards laid out in October by the Assistant Secretary of War for Energy, Installations, and Environment, Mark Dale . The new guidelines classify barracks maintenance work orders into three categories: emergency, urgent and routine. 

The memo did not provide specific examples of what scenarios would classify under the three categories. Barracks have become a highly scrutinized quality-of-life issue in recent years, with troops facing problems that range from mold and pest infestations impacting their health to serious safety concerns as well as more routine nuisances like broken air conditioners in hot climates and delayed maintenance on aging buildings .

The military services were told to inspect barracks by Monday and take actions to address “emergency conditions” within 24 hours, which includes providing troops with temporary quarters if their room isn’t “safe” enough to live in.

Rob Evans, founder of the barracks review app, Hots&Cots , and an advocate for junior enlisted housing, said the urgency behind these instructions is right, but “service members have been through this before.”

In October 2025, the Department of Defense launched the Barracks Task Force to address subpar housing conditions for junior enlisted service members. By December 2025, the Pentagon announced that it had completed…
items.t: Troops in unsafe barracks can get temporary housing on or off base, Pentagon says

items.title: Mysterious New B94 Nuclear Bomb Designation Emerges, First In Decades
items.summary:
The Senate Appropriations Committee has revealed the first entirely new designation for an air-dropped nuclear gravity bomb in decades. What the B94 bomb is remains to be confirmed. The only weapon fitting this general description known to be in development now is the bunker-busting Nuclear Deterrent System-Air-delivered (NDS-A).

The B94 designation appears in an explanatory statement that the Senate Appropriations Committee released last week. The document accompanied a draft bill covering proposed funding for the Department of Energy and certain other arms of the federal government in Fiscal Year 2027.

Jeffery Lewis, currently the William J. Perry Lecturer at Stanford University’s Center for International Security and Cooperation (CISAC) and Distinguished Fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) think tank, was among the first to call attention to the designation in a post on X . He, in turn, credited Eliana Johns, a PhD student at the University of Maryland and a Research Advisor at the Federation of American Scientists (FAS) think tank, for having spotted it first.

items.title: ‘Davidson Window’ Admiral Hopes He Was Wrong On China’s Ability To Take Taiwan By 2027
items.summary:
The man whose congressional testimony five years ago led to what’s known as the “Davidson Window” for China being capable of launching a credible invasion of Taiwan by 2027 is offering some insights into what he is thinking now that the date is drawing near. 

Philip Davidson – the admiral who led U.S. forces in the Pacific at the time – said on a podcast released Friday that several developments have taken place since he retired in 2021 that could change his projection. However, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (now Pacific Command or PACOM) told the Why Should We Care About the Indo-Pacific? podcast he still sees reasons for concern. In particular, he urged the U.S. to deliver military aid to Taiwan before an invasion to better deter China from acting.

Chinese forces practice a beach landing. (PLA) 

Davidson’s statements were delivered as China has been steadily increasing military exercises around Taiwan , which it considers a breakaway province that it will someday bring back under its control.

Before getting into what Davidson told podcasters Ray Powell, founder and executive director of the SeaLight Foundation , and Jim Carouso, a senior advisor at BowerGroupAsia , let’s recall what Davidson told the Senate Armed Services Committee on March 9, 2021.

“I worry that they are accelerating their ambitions to supplant the United States, and our leadership role in the rules-based international order, which they have long said that they want to do that by 2050, I am worried about them moving that target closer,” Davidson said of China. “Taiwan is clearly…
items.t: ‘Davidson Window’ Admiral Hopes He Was Wrong On China’s Ability To Take Taiwan By 2027

items.title: Trident nuclear submarine concludes record underwater deployment
items.summary:
HMS Vengeance’s seven-month patrol prompts fears over slow pace of maintenance of ageing fleet and strain on crew

A Trident nuclear submarine has concluded a record seven-month deployment, returning to the Faslane naval base in Scotland where its crew was greeted by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting.

HMS Vengeance began its patrol on 12 April and spent 217 days submerged before returning on Sunday, having left the country when Keir Starmer was in Downing Street and Manchester United were third in the Premier League.

The debate over impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has largely drowned out discussion of the professional military education (PME) reforms he rolled out on Monday in a 33-point memorandum and a companion speech at the Naval War College. 

For the uninitiated, PME is the blanket term for a series of educational opportunities provided to service members as they progress through their military careers. For officers, this educational sequence extends from commissioning—whether from a military academy, the Reserve Officers Training Corps (ROTC), or Officer Candidate School—all the way up through capstone programs for generals and flag officers. These educational experiences prepare our military leaders for the growing responsibilities they will shoulder as they move up the ladder, from commanding a couple dozen service members as a junior officer to a few thousand as a colonel or a Navy captain.

items.summary:

On Sunday, the 18th Wing said that the first F-15EX, with new electronic warfare systems, was delivered to the base. Kadena is the first overseas U.S. base to get the fighter jet.

It’s an exciting time to be part of the 67th Fighter Squadron.”

items.title: Soldiers in Poland are barred from karaoke, strip clubs and disturbing wildlife
items.summary:
Soldiers serving under V Corps in Europe are directed to not visit bars, strip clubs, night clubs as a whole as well as karaoke or hookah lounges, the formation’s leadership said this month. 

The Army’s V Corps announced the expanded rules earlier in November, as part of an update to orders covering a sweeping range of prohibitions for soldiers. The directives, which also include rules against buying electronic cigarettes from unauthorized vendors and orders not to disturb wildlife, were done to preserve “good order, discipline, and the safety of our personnel,” a V Corps spokesperson told Task & Purpose.

The new order, issued Nov. 5 and effective immediately, replaces an existing version issued August 2024 . It was signed by Lt. Gen. Thomas Feltey, who took over command of V Corps this fall. The order applies to soldiers under V Corps, not just in Poland but those assigned to 15 other European nations.

Feltey’s order notes that “common sense and good judgment” should be used when evaluating if an establishment is considered off limits. If they aren’t sure, soldiers have a “duty” to get clarity from their leaders. The order takes the time to differentiate each type of establishment.

The FAA has made the very rare move of halting all flights across the country. The agency announced that communications issues are to blame.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. 

In January 2023, the FAA halted flights because of issues with a pilot alert system. Before that, traffic was halted nationwide after the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.

items.title: Navy relieves commander of destroyer USS Michael Murphy
items.summary:
The Navy quietly relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham, skipper of the guided-missile destroyer USS Michael Murphy, on Sept. 27 “due to a loss of confidence to command,” a Navy official told Task & Purpose.

The relief came nine months into the ship’s 11-month deployment to the Middle East, where the USS Michael Murphy helped enforce a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, escort tankers, launch Tomahawk cruise missiles, and defend against Iranian drone and missile attacks. The USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group, which the Murphy was a part of, was later awarded the Presidential Unit Citation. 

USNI News first reported on Cunningham’s removal .

No reason was given for Cunningham’s firing. The Navy regularly uses the term “loss of confidence” as a catchall for the many reasons a commander can be relieved. The term is used for everything from mishaps onboard the vessel to personal misconduct by an officer. 

Cmdr. David Nicholas has helmed the destroyer since Cunningham was relieved.

items.title: The Pentagon brings back World War II-era OSS for special operations missions, funding

The Office of Strategic Services, the intelligence and commando arm of the U.S. military during World War II, might live again, at least in name, as part of a reorganization of the Pentagon’s special operations civilian leadership. 

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memo on Nov. 2 that renames the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict to the Assistant Secretary of War for the Office of Strategic Services, though permanently doing so would require congressional approval. 

As part of the renaming, Hegseth wants to move the assistant secretary of defense for special operations and low-intensity conflict position higher up the leadership ladder, marking the latest in a decades-long effort to put civilian oversight of special operations forces (SOF) on an even footing with the secretaries of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.

items.title: Destroyer That Has Been Deployed Longer Than Any Since WWII Returns Home
items.summary:
Two guided-missile destroyers assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group (CSG), USS Spruance and USS Michael Murphy , have returned home after 357- and 346-day deployments, respectively, more than a month after the carrier they escorted returned to San Diego . Both are reportedly longer than any previous destroyer cruise since World War II. However, the record may not hold for long, as USS John Finn is on pace to surpass both.

Spruance pulled out of Naval Base San Diego on November 21, 2025, alongside Nimitz class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln , on what the crews expected would be a routine deployment to the Western Pacific. Murphy linked up with the strike group 10 days later as it sailed past her homeport at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii.

Both ships, which endured conditions just as grueling as Lincoln , if not more so, returned to their homeports over the past 24 hours. Spruance departed Pearl Harbor on November 6, according to MarineTraffic , and arrived in San Diego today. Planet Labs satellite imagery reviewed by TWZ showed Murphy in Guam on November 3, her last stop before transiting northeast back to Pearl Harbor and pulling into port yesterday.

USS Michael Murphy returns home to Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam on November 12. U.S. Navy photo 

The extended deployments are a reminder of how the war with Iran and the blockade that followed have pushed the Navy’s surface fleet past the seven-month cruises it long treated as standard. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle told Sailors recently to expect the new normal for deployments…
items.t: Destroyer That Has Been Deployed Longer Than Any Since WWII Returns Home

The Air Force and Northrop Grumman announced the start of B-21 weapons testing in separate press releases. 

“During the test, a B-21 test aircraft flying from Edwards Air Force Base, California, released a conventional weapon, validating its digital models and the maturity of its open systems architecture,” according to the Air Force . “This test proves the B-21’s strike capability, proves its ability to rapidly onboard new weapons and solidifies its role as the future backbone of the U.S. bomber fleet.”

A stock picture of a pre-production B-21 Raider bomber during a past flight test. USAF 

The Air Force’s release does not name the munition in question or provide any more context about the release. The B-21 is intended to carry a wide variety of conventional and nuclear munitions. The still-in-development AGM-181A Long Range Stand-Off (LRSO) nuclear-armed cruise missile is set to be a particularly key part of the Raider’s arsenal. 

At the time of writing, no images of the bomber actually dropping anything have been released. From what has been seen previously, the B-21 looks to have a single large central weapons bay compared to the two side-by-side bays on the existing B-2 Spirit. It has been kept secret for decades, buried four metres deep into the white cliffs of Dover. But from Friday, members of the public will finally be able to visit a pioneering command bunker that was ordered by Winston Churchill and proved a vital defence during the second world war.

The Fan Bay plotting room, which is encased in concrete, housed the first land-based computer-aided targeting system. items.title: Ukraine Says Starshield Disruptions Are Back As U.S. Negotiators Meet With Putin
items.summary:
For the second time in a month , Ukrainian officials and military personnel are complaining that weapons using SpaceX’s vital Starshield satellite communications system have had limits placed on the speeds at which they can operate. The officials say the latest Starshield issues are impairing Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile barrages and strike targets far behind the lines in Ukrainian territory that Russia holds. Ukrainians made similar claims in October, and the service was eventually restored .

The complaints, from President Volodymyr Zelensky, one of his main advisors, and frontline troops, are being made as U.S. negotiators met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in another White House-brokered effort to end the war. Some Ukrainians are reportedly even claiming the Starshield system is being impacted to pressure Ukraine to bend to Russian demands to give up territory. 

SpaceX denied the allegations.

“This is false,” a SpaceX official told us. “There has been no change.”

A Ukrainian soldier of the 61st Separate Mechanized Brigade uses the Starlink system. (Photo by Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto via Getty Images) NurPhoto 

While TWZ cannot independently verify the Ukrainian claims about Starshield, the issue again highlights the challenges Kyiv faces fighting a war while relying on donated equipment and services. The country is working on alternatives, including developing its own satellite communications system . However, even Ukrainian officials acknowledge that it won’t come close to replacing the SpaceX system.

items.title: GOP tries to speed-walk search for GAO's next chief
items.summary:
A lame-duck Congress is suddenly hastening the process to find a new long-term leader of a governmentwide watchdog agency that has drawn the ire of the Trump administration. 

House and Senate Republicans faced calls over the past two years to start the bipartisan process of interviewing candidates to lead the Government Accountability Office. 

Under the current process, the selection of the GAO comptroller general begins with a commission of 10 senior House and Senate lawmakers from both parties that recommends individuals for the position to the president. 

Whoever the president selects is subject to Senate confirmation for one nonrenewable 15-year term. The last time lawmakers vetted candidates for GAO’s top job in 2010, the congressional commission spent more than a year on its search. 

This time around, members of the commission are being given a single day to come up with candidate recommendations, after receiving notice on Veterans Day. The commission is meant to recommend at least three candidates for the job. 

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., requested commission members on Wednesday to submit candidates to serve as GAO’s next comptroller general within a 24-hour deadline, according to top congressional Democrats who
items.t: GOP tries to speed-walk search for GAO's next chief

items.title: Vets groups slam House for quietly passing divisive benefits bill on Veterans Day
items.summary:
A divisive bill that cuts disability benefits for veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus while simultaneously granting compensation for combat veterans was passed by the House on Veterans Day — evoking condemnation from Democrats and veterans groups.

The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act is a large legislative package with dozens of bills, including a controversial set of policies that drew strong opposition from the start. Veteran Service Organizations said that the package would cut disability benefits from one group — veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus ratings — and act as an “offset” to pay for another group, combat wounded veterans.

Democrats and veteran advocates criticized House Republicans for passing disability cuts on Veterans Day — and doing so with a voice vote where members call out “aye” or “no” the loudest, instead of recording an official vote under their name. 

“On a day when America honors the brave men and women who stepped forward to defend our freedom, House leaders chose to sneak through legislation threatening earned benefits for millions of veterans, their families and survivors,” Disabled American Veterans National Commander John Donovan said in a statement. “Veterans risked their lives to guarantee our right to vote, and those who have the privilege of serving in Congress should have the backbone and decency to openly stand behind their votes, not hide like thieves in the night.”

Republicans declared the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act passage a “historic healthcare and benefits expansion,” noting that the bill gets rid of limits for…
items.t: Vets groups slam House for quietly passing divisive benefits bill on Veterans Day

items.title: L-39NG Skyfox Jets Could Give Ukraine A Critical New Russian Drone Hunting Capability
items.summary:
The Czech Republic could supply Ukraine with up to 16 Aero L-39NG Skyfox aircraft, potentially giving Kyiv another option for countering Russia’s Shahed-type attack drones . The proposal includes four aircraft previously agreed to for transfer and 12 more that Czech officials are now discussing with their Ukrainian counterparts.

Czech Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček raised the expanded arrangement during a visit to Kyiv yesterday, where he met Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi. Havlíček described the discussions as encouraging but did not announce a finalized agreement for the additional aircraft.

L-39NG Skyfox. Aero Vodochody 

Skyfox is based on the Cold War-era Aero L-39 Albatros jet trainer, a rugged and reliable Soviet aircraft that was produced in the thousands and served all over the globe. The new L-39NG was reworked and modernized in the 2010s in an effort to recapture jet trainer market share that had waned as the Soviet design was increasingly passed over for more modern alternatives. Many L-39s are also flown privately in the United States and are used for contracted air support services for the U.S. military. One of the firms that uses them, Draken International , actually assisted in the L-39NG project and acted as a U.S. anchor for the program.

The Skyfox’s redesigned structure makes use of modern materials, reducing weight and increasing structural lifespan to 15,000 flight hours. The American Williams FJ44-4M turbofan, a very widely used jet engine that is found on many private jets, replaces the original…
items.t: L-39NG Skyfox Jets Could Give Ukraine A Critical New Russian Drone Hunting Capability

items.title: New Facilities To Pump Out Upgraded F/A-18E/F Super Hornets Eyed By Navy
items.summary:
The U.S. Navy is looking for new avenues to bolster its pipelines for major F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler modifications. The prime contractor for that work now, Boeing, is in the process of expanding and reorganizing its production infrastructure . At the same time, the company’s defense business arm is also heavily focused on ramping up output of new aircraft, including the sixth-generation F-47 for the U.S. Air Force and the Navy’s next-generation carrier-based F/A-XX fighter . 

Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR) is now “conducting market research to determine the industrial base’s existing capability and facility capacity to provide supplemental or secondary Service Life Modification (SLM) turnkey capacity for F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler aircraft starting in FY29 [Fiscal Year 2029],” according to a contracting notice put out earlier this week . “To support long-term strike fighter inventory requirements, the Government is evaluating the availability of additional commercial or second-source depot modification repair overhaul (MRO) capacity.”

Currently, Boeing performs Service Life Modification (SLM) work on Navy F/A-18E/Fs at facilities in St. Louis, Missouri, and San Antonio, Texas. The Navy has its own Super Hornet SLM line, operated in cooperation with Boeing, at the Fleet Readiness Center Southwest (FRCSW) depot in San Diego, California. Boeing conducts additional F/A-18E/F and EA-18G modification work at various facilities, including an additional site in Jacksonville, Florida. 

Workers move a US Navy F/A-18F Super Hornet at Boeing’s…
items.t: New Facilities To Pump Out Upgraded F/A-18E/F Super Hornets Eyed By Navy

items.title: Soldier receives Bronze Star for Valor for ‘fearless actions’ after drone strike at start of Iran war
items.summary:
The Army recently published a series of photos of an award ceremony for a soldier credited with saving lives following an Iranian drone strike on U.S. troops in Kuwait at the start of the Iran war. 

Sgt. 1st Class Oscar M. McGrew was awarded a Bronze Star with “V” device for valor during an Oct. 23 award ceremony at Fort Hood, Texas. The images, which were uploaded on Oct. 26 to the military’s image database , mark one of the rare instances in the ongoing conflict where an enlisted soldier has received the award for valor.

Task & Purpose was the first to report that Sgt. 1st Class Oscar M. McGrew had been recognized for his response during the March 1 Iranian one-way drone and ballistic missile attack on Port Shuaiba, Kuwait.

The attack was part of a series of Iranian retaliatory strikes on American bases around the Middle East in the opening hours of the war. The strike killed six Army Reserve soldiers and injured more . To date, it remains the deadliest of the war.

The Army confirmed to Task & Purpose in September that McGrew was the Directorate of Logistics noncommissioned officer-in-charge for Area Support Group-Kuwait. 

Sgt. 1st Class Oscar McGrew, center, during the award ceremony at Cooper Field on Fort Hood, Texas, Oct. 23, 2026. Army photo by Spc. Michelle Lessard-Terry. 

Captions for the photos of the award ceremony identify McGrew as a member of the 215th Brigade Support Battalion, 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team.

“His fearless actions directly saved lives and prevented further casualties during an active enemy attack,” the photo caption reads.

items.t: Soldier receives Bronze Star for Valor for ‘fearless actions’ after drone strike at start of Iran war

items.title: 'Robot Wars': Defense One Futures, Ep. 1
items.summary:
Welcome to Defense One Futures, our new podcast about the people and technology shaping the future of national security. In this debut episode, we explore how robotic autonomy is altering warfare, with firsthand accounts of how the U.S. military and NATO allies are rethinking every aspect of buying, building, and training in the age of autonomy and AI.

At North Carolina’s Fort Bragg and Alabama’s Clark Range, the U.S. Army is incorporating advanced battlefield robotics into training. Across the Atlantic, NATO in September completed a large maritime exercise focused on coordinated, autonomous operations.

items.title: Air Force aims for year-round operations at three Pacific islands
items.summary:
The Air Force intends to use four airfields in the Pacific for more than 6,000 aerial operations per year, as part of its expanding operations in the region.

Calling it a “unique opportunity” to support new operational objectives, the Air Force plans to use Saipan International Airport, Tinian International Airport, Tinian North Field and Rota International Airport, all located in the Northern Mariana Islands, for thousands of training flights and aerial exercises per year. The operations are meant to support the service’s Agile Combat Employment, or ACE, strategy, which aims to disperse aerial operations over several locations to avoid creating one large target.

The plan was announced in a notice of intent published late in October. The notice calls for getting environmental impact statements on plans to stage aircraft on the three Pacific islands.

items.title: Air Force buying up to 16,000 new helmets to replace 40-year-old model
items.summary:
The Air Force is buying new helmets for fixed-wing aviators that are said to be lighter, better ventilated, and more adaptable to new technology than the current helmet — the HGU-55/P — that’s been in use for more than 40 years.

On Nov. 5, LIFT Airborne Technologies announced it was awarded a 10-year contract with the Air Force for its AV2.2 Next Generation Fixed Wing Helmet system. The contract is worth up to $83.4 million and up to 16,000 helmets, which would be more than enough for all the commissioned fixed-wing aviators in the active-duty Air Force.

And Air Force spokesman told Task & Purpose that the service expects deliveries of the helmet to begin in late summer 2027, with the goal of reaching initial operational capability that September.

The one fixed-wing community not included in the contract are F-35 fighter pilots, who have their own brain buckets that cost about as much as a Ferrari . All other fixed-wing aviators have worn the HGU-55/P since the 1980s . 

But times are changing, and the Air Force said it needs different gear to help aircrew stay healthy and to keep up with new technology. That said, it is not clear at this time which units will receive the helmets first.

Pain in the neck 

The HGU-55/P weighs about 2.2 pounds. That may not sound like much, but the pounds add up in high-G maneuvers. A human head weighs about 10 or 11 pounds. That plus a two-pound helmet, plus the weight of any attached heads-up displays or night-vision goggles, and it totals about 120 pounds sitting on the pilot’s neck in a 9G turn.
